title: CEOs Who Built Their Empires on Lies and Blood
fullText: Number one, Elizabeth Holmes. The fraud she built did not collapse with a bang. It dissolved slowly, molecule by molecule, like the blood samples her machines were supposed to analyze, but never could. When the dust finally settled on Therronos, what remained was not merely a failed company. It was a permanent scar across the face of Silicon Valley, a wound in the national conversation about innovation, ambition, and the line between vision and deception. Lawmakers would rewrite oversight standards. Investors who had entrusted hundreds of millions of dollars to a woman once hailed as the next Steve Jobs would spend years in litigation trying to recoup pennies of what they had lost. And patients who had received inaccurate blood test results, some of them critically ill, were left wondering whether the treatments their doctors had prescribed based on faulty data had done them more harm than good. The consequences of Elizabeth Holmes radiated outward like cracks in glass, and they have not finished spreading. She was born on February 3rd, 1984 in Washington, D.C. into a family that understood the mechanics of American power. Her father, Christian Holmes, held executive positions across the federal government, including roles at USAD, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the United States Trade and Development Agency. Before that, he had been a vice president at Enron, a company whose own spectacular fraud would one day serve as a dark parallel to his daughter's story. Her mother, Noel Dowst, worked as a congressional committee staffer. On both sides of the family, there was wealth and lineage. The Holmes family descended from Charles Louie Fleshman, a Hungarian immigrant who had founded Fleshman's Chist and built one of the great American industrial fortunes of the 19th century. A family friend once said the Holmes family was proud of that history, proud of the yeast empire, and that Elizabeth had channeled the ambition to reclaim that status from a very young age. She attended St. John's school in Houston, one of the city's most prestigious private institutions, where she distinguished herself through determination rather than warmth. She was not remembered as particularly sociable. She was remembered as relentless. While still in high school, she taught herself Mandarin Chinese and began attending Stanford University's summer language programs. She claimed to have started a business selling C++ compilers to Chinese universities before she had even graduated. Whether or not that claim was entirely accurate, it established a pattern that would follow her for the next two decades. Elizabeth Holmes understood from a remarkably young age the power of narrative. She understood that the story you told about yourself could be more important than the product you actually built. In 2002, she enrolled at Stanford University to study chemical engineering. After her freshman year, she worked in a laboratory at the Genome Institute of Singapore, where she tested blood samples for the SARS Corona virus. It was there, she would later say, that the seed of Theronos was planted. She was troubled by the cumbersome process of drawing large volumes of blood with syringes. She imagined a future in which all of that could be replaced by a single finger prick. A tiny drop of blood analyzed on a portable device capable of running hundreds of tests simultaneously. The vision was intoxicating. It was also, as multiple experts told her at the time, scientifically implausible. When Holmes pitched the idea to Phyllis Gardner, a professor of medicine at Stanford, Gardner told her directly that the concept would not work. The biochemistry of blood simply did not support the idea that meaningful diagnostic results could be derived from such small samples. Several other medical experts at the university said the same thing. Holmes ignored them all. She found one supporter, Channing Robertson, a dean at Stanford's School of Engineering, who agreed to back her vision. In March 2004, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford, used her tuition money as seed funding, and founded the company that would eventually be called Therronos. The name was a combination of the words therapy and diagnosis. The original name realtime cures had been scrapped because too many people were skeptical of the word cure. Even at the naming stage, Holmes was already managing perception. By December 2004, Holmes had raised $6 million. By 2010, Therronos had attracted more than $92 million in venture capital. The technology was still not working, but the money kept coming because the story was irresistible. A young, brilliant woman, dropout from Stanford, challenging the entrenched laboratory industry, democratizing health care for ordinary people. Holmes cultivated the image carefully. She began wearing black turtleneck sweaters, a deliberate homage to Steve Jobs. She adopted a deep baritone voice during public appearances, a vocal affectation that multiple former colleagues and Stanford acquaintances would later confirm was not her natural speaking voice. She surrounded herself with powerful people, building a board of directors that included former secretaries of state Henry Kissinger and George Schultz, former Secretary of Defense William Perry, future Secretary of Defense James Mattis. retired Navy admirals, former senators from both parties, and former CEOs of Wells Fargo and Becttel. In 2015, Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire in America based on a $9 billion valuation of Theronos. Time included her in its list of the 100 most influential people in the world. President Barack Obama appointed her a presidential ambassador for global entrepreneurship. None of the celebrated board members had a background in laboratory science or diagnostic medicine. That was not an accident. Holmes needed authority figures who would lend her credibility, not experts who might ask difficult questions about the technology. The technology, as it turned out, did not work. The company's proprietary device called the Edison was never able to reliably perform the range of tests Therronos claimed. Internally, the company resorted to running most of its tests on commercially available machines manufactured by other companies, including devices made by Seammens. Even those results were often unreliable because the blood samples were too small and had to be diluted, which introduced errors. Employees who raised concerns about the accuracy of the tests were marginalized or fired. The company operated under a culture of secrecy and fear driven in large part by Holmes and her romantic partner and chief operating officer Romesh Balwani. Balwani who was 19 years older than Holmes and had been romantically involved with her since she was 18 wielded enormous control inside Theronos. Together they maintained an atmosphere in which dissent was treated as betrayal. The unraveling began in 2015 when journalist John Kerru of the Wall Street Journal received a tip from a medical expert who was suspicious of Theronos's claims. Kerru spent months conducting a secret investigation, interviewing former employees and obtaining internal documents. When Holmes learned of the investigation, she deployed her attorney, David Boy, to threaten the journal and the whistleblowers with legal action. Boy sent intimidating letters, attempted to shut down sources, and tried everything in his considerable legal arsenal to kill the story. It did not work. In October 2015, the journal published Kerru's investigation, revealing that the Edison device produced inaccurate results and that Theronos had been using commercially available machines for most of its testing. Holmes responded with defiance. She called the journal a tabloid. She went on CNBC's Mad Money and told Jim Kramer that criticism was simply what happened when you tried to change the world. She quoted a version of a line often attributed to Mahatma Gandhi about first being ignored, then being fought, then winning. But the ground was already shifting beneath her. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services inspected the company's laboratory in Newark, California, and found serious irregularities. By July 2016, regulators had banned homes from owning or operating a blood testing service for 2 years. Walgreens, which had partnered with Theronos to open instore blood collection centers, severed its relationship with the company. The Food and Drug Administration ordered Theronos to stop using one of its core inventions. The state of Arizona filed suit, alleging that Theronos had sold 1.5 million blood tests to consumers while concealing the truth about those tests. In March 2018, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Holmes and Balwani with fraud, alleging that they had raised over $700 million from investors through false and exaggerated claims. Among the lies was Therronos's claim that its technology was being used by the United States Department of Defense in combat zones. The company had also told investors it was generating $100 million in annual revenue. The actual figure for 2014 was $100,000. Holmes settled the SEC's civil charges by paying a $500,000 fine returning shares and accepting a 10-year ban from serving as an officer or director of any public company. But the civil settlement was only the beginning. In June 2018, a federal grand jury indicted Holmes and Balwani on nine counts of wire fraud and two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Both pleaded not guilty. The criminal trial delayed by the pandemic and by Holmes's pregnancy began in August 2021 in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California. The trial lasted months. Holmes testified in her own defense for 7 days. She claimed she was misled by her own staff about the technology. She also claimed that Balwani had exerted undue control over her, including emotional and sexual abuse during their yearslong relationship. The defense strategy was in essence to portray Holmes as a victim rather than a mastermind. The prosecution presented evidence of fabricated reports, staged demonstrations for investors, falsified validation data, and a systematic campaign of deception that Holmes had personally directed. On January 3rd, 2022, the jury found Holmes guilty on four counts of defrauding investors, including three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy. She was acquitted on four counts related to defrauding patients. On November 18th, 2022, Judge Edward Dila sentenced her to 11 years and three months in federal prison and ordered her and Balwani to jointly pay $452 million in restitution. Holmes reported to federal prison camp Brian in Texas on May 30, 2023. The reverberations of Therronos extended far beyond one woman and one company. The case fundamentally altered how Silicon Valley vets biotech startups. Investors who had once taken the word of charismatic founders on faith began demanding to see actual data, actual results, actual proof that the technology worked before writing checks. The regulatory apparatus that had failed to catch the fraud early enough came under withering scrutiny. Kerr's reporting and subsequent book bad blood became a defining document of an era in which hype and disruption had been confused with genuine innovation. Lawmakers cited Theronos in hearings about corporate accountability and consumer protection. Romesh Balwani tried separately was convicted on all 12 felony counts against him and sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison. The combined sentences sent a message, but for many of the people affected, it was not enough. The investors who had lost hundreds of millions included some of the wealthiest families in America. Rupert Murdoch lost more than $100 million. The Walton family, the Devos family, and Carlos Slim were all among the victims. But the human cost extended beyond money. Patients in Arizona and elsewhere had received blood test results that were wrong. Some had been told they had conditions they did not have. Others had been told they were healthy when they were not. The full scope of the medical harm caused by Theronos may never be fully known. Holmes appealed her conviction. In February 2025, the Ninth Circuit rejected every argument her lawyers raised and affirmed both the conviction and the sentence. She remains incarcerated. The story she told about herself, the story about a fearless young woman who would revolutionize medicine, turned out to be the most dangerous product Theronos ever created. The machinery of law and regulation eventually caught up to her. But the damage she left behind to patients, to investors, to public trust, to the very idea that technology can solve the world's problems has proven far more difficult to repair than anyone anticipated. Number two, Sam Bankman Fried. The bankruptcy filing alone ran to more than 130 affiliated entities. That number is worth pausing on. When FTX collapsed in November 2022, it was not a single company that fell. It was a sprawling interconnected web of exchanges, trading firms, venture investments, and shell entities that had been built with stunning speed and virtually no internal controls. The man who had constructed this architecture was 30 years old. He had been on the cover of Forbes. He had been called the JP Morgan of crypto. Members of Congress had invited him to testify as a trusted voice on regulation. Charitable organizations had received tens of millions of his dollars. And when it all came apart, the courtappointed administrator who replaced him, the same attorney who had overseen the liquidation of Enron, said he had never in his career seen such a complete failure of corporate governance or such a total absence of trustworthy financial information. The aftermath of Sam Bankman fried reshaped the regulatory landscape for an entire industry, accelerated the collapse of multiple other crypto firms, and left millions of ordinary people unable to access their own money. Samuel Benjamin Bankman Fried was born on March 5th, 1992 on the campus of Stanford University. Both of his parents were professors at Stanford Law School. His mother, Barbara Frerieded, was a specialist in tax law and political philosophy. His father, Joseph Bankman, was an expert on tax policy and behavioral economics. His aunt was the dean of Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health. He grew up in an environment saturated with intellectual rigor and ethical abstraction, surrounded by conversations about utilitarianism, effective altruism, and the moral obligation to maximize good in the world. These ideas would later become central to his public persona, and central to the defense he would eventually mount in court. He attended Crystal Springs Upland School in Hillsboro, California, a private institution known for its academic intensity. As a teenager, he participated in Canada USA Math Camp, a summer program for mathematically gifted students. He enrolled at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology where he majored in physics with a minor in mathematics. At MIT, he lived in a cooperative housing group called epsilon Theta. He was not known for his social skills or personal hygiene. He was known for playing video games during meetings, for sleeping on beanag chairs, and for a restless, almost frenetic energy that those around him interpreted as brilliance. During the summer of 2013, Bankman Fried interned at Jane Street Capital, a quantitative trading firm in New York. After graduating from MIT in 2014, he returned to Jane Street full-time. He traded international exchange traded funds and developed a reputation for processing risk quickly. He earned a substantial salary and began donating roughly half of it to charity in keeping with the principles of effective altruism. the philosophical movement arguing that people should use evidence and reason to determine how to do the most good. He had become deeply immersed in the movement through the writings of philosopher William Macascal. In late 2017, Bankman Fried left Jane Street and co-founded Alama Research, a quantitative cryptocurrency trading firm. His early profits came from exploiting price differences in Bitcoin between exchanges in different countries, a practice known as arbitrage. He moved the operation to Hong Kong in late 2018. And in April 2019, he founded FTX, a cryptocurrency derivatives exchange that quickly grew into one of the largest and most prominent platforms in the industry. FTX expanded with breathtaking speed. By 2021, it had more than a million users and had reached a valuation of $32 billion. Bankman Fried became one of the wealthiest people in America with a net worth estimated at over $26 billion at its peak. He appeared on the Forbes 400. He gave interviews to every major financial outlet. He testified before Congress. He donated lavishly to political campaigns, overwhelmingly to Democrats. though he later admitted that he had also made large donations to Republican causes through intermediaries to avoid public attention. He signed the giving pledge, promising to donate the majority of his wealth. He funded pandemic prevention research. He became the public face of responsible crypto. Behind the public image, however, the machinery was already breaking down. The core of the fraud was the relationship between FTX and Alama Research. Bankman Fried controlled both entities. FTX customers deposited their money into the exchange believing it was being held safely. In reality, billions of dollars in customer funds were being funneled to Alama Research, which used the money to make risky investments, repay loans, purchase real estate in the Bahamas, and make political donations. The mechanism was deceptively simple. Alama had been granted a virtually unlimited line of credit on FTX, exempt from the collateral requirements that applied to every other user. Senior engineers testified that they had implemented this feature at Bankman Fried's direction. In addition, before FTX had its own bank accounts, customer deposits in traditional currency had been routed through Alama. Billions of dollars flowed in and were never properly tracked or returned. By the time the scheme unraveled, Alama owed FTX approximately $10 billion, money that belonged to FTX customers. The collapse came suddenly in November 2022. Coindesk published a report revealing that the majority of Alama Research's balance sheet consisted of FTT, a token created by FTX itself. The report raised serious questions about whether Alama was solvent. Changpang Xiao, the CEO of Binance, FTX's largest competitor, announced publicly that Binance would sell its substantial holdings of FTT. The announcement triggered a bank run. FTX customers rushed to withdraw their funds. Within days, FTX could not meet the demand. On November 8th, Bankman Fried tweeted that FTX was fine and that assets were fine they were not. On November 11th, 2022, FTX, Alama Research, and more than 130 affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy. Bankman Fried resigned as CEO. John Ray 3, the restructuring expert, who had handled the Enron bankruptcy, was appointed to manage the proceedings. In a sworn declaration, Ry stated that he had never encountered such a complete absence of financial controls. There were no reliable records, no separation between corporate and personal funds, no independent board oversight, no functioning compliance department. Bankman Fried was arrested in the Bahamas on December 12th, 2022 and extradited to the United States. He was charged with seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. He pleaded not guilty. He was released on a $250 million bond, the largest in American criminal history, and confined to his parents' home in California. While awaiting trial, his bail conditions were tightened after he contacted potential witnesses. He was eventually jailed before trial after the judge found he had tampered with witnesses. The trial began on October 3rd, 2023 in Manhattan. Three of Bankman Fried's closest associates, Caroline Ellison, Gary Wang, and Nishad Singh, had already pleaded guilty and agreed to cooperate with the prosecution. Ellison, who had served as CEO of Alama Research and had been Bankman Fried's romantic partner, testified that she had prepared false balance sheets at his direction and that Bankman Fried was aware that FTX customer funds were being used by Alamita. Wang, the co-founder of FTX, testified that he had manipulated computer code to allow Alamita's unlimited access to customer accounts. The defense argued that Bankman Fried was a well-meaning but overwhelmed entrepreneur who had made mistakes but had not intended to commit fraud. On November 2nd, 2023, the jury found him guilty on all seven counts. On March 28th, 2024, Bankman Fried was sentenced to 25 years in federal prison and ordered to forfeit 11 billion. The sentence was intended to account not just for the money stolen, but for the scale of the deception, the number of victims, and the systematic nature of the fraud. The fallout of FTX extended far beyond one company and one defendant. The collapse accelerated a broader crisis in the cryptocurrency industry, contributing to the failure of multiple lending platforms and exchanges. Regulatory agencies around the world intensified their scrutiny of crypto markets. In the United States, the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission dramatically expanded their enforcement actions. The political donations Bankman Freud had made became a source of embarrassment for the recipients. His funding of effective altruism organizations created a crisis within that movement as members struggled with the realization that much of their recent growth had been financed with stolen money. The court proceedings exposed the fragility of an industry that had been built largely on trust and narrative rather than on audited financials and regulatory compliance. Bankman Fried appealed his conviction in April 2024. He remains incarcerated. The trust that had been the foundation of his empire, the trust of investors, of regulators, of philanthropists, of millions of ordinary customers who had believed their money was safe, proved to be the most consequential casualty of his fraud. Number three, Kenneth Lei. He died before they could sentence him. That fact alone ensured that the legal legacy of Kenneth Lei would remain incomplete. A story that reached its climax in the courtroom, but was denied its final chapter by a heart attack on a Colorado mountainside. Under American law, when a defendant dies during a pending appeal, the conviction is typically vacated. And so the man who presided over the most devastating corporate fraud of his era, the man whose company's collapse destroyed 20,000 jobs, erased more than $60 billion in shareholder value, and wiped out the retirement savings of thousands of ordinary workers, was technically, legally never convicted of anything. The judgment was erased, but the damage was not. Enron's collapse reshaped corporate law in the United States. It led directly to the Sarbain Oxley Act, the most sweeping overhaul of financial regulation since the New Deal. It changed how Americans understood the relationship between executive power, accounting transparency, and the fragility of public trust. And the name Kenneth Lei became permanently synonymous with the cost of that failure. He was born on April 15th, 1942 in the small town of Tyrone, Missouri, deep in the rural poverty of the Ozarks. His father, Omar Lei, was a Baptist preacher. His mother, Ruth, ran the household. The family's general store had failed, and the Lays lived modestly, sometimes precariously. Kenneth Lay grew up understanding scarcity, and he spent the rest of his life running from it. He was an excellent student. He attended the University of Missouri where he studied economics, earning a bachelor's degree in 1964 and a master's degree in 1965. He went on to earn a doctorate in economics from the University of Houston in 1970. Between those degrees, he served as a lieutenant in the United States Navy, working as a financial analyst at the Pentagon. His early career was a model of institutional ambition. He worked at Humble Oil, the precursor to Exxon, as a corporate economist. He served as a technical assistant to the Federal Power Commission and as deputy under secretary of the Department of the Interior under the Nixon administration. He understood energy policy from the inside. When the deregulation of American energy markets began in the 1980s, Lei was already positioned at the intersection of government and industry. In 1984, he became chairman and CEO of Houston Natural Gas Company. When Omaha based Interorth acquired Houston Natural Gas in 1985, the combined entity was renamed Enron and Lei took the helm. Under Lay's leadership, Enron transformed from a conventional pipeline and energy company into something unprecedented. A trading powerhouse that bought and sold not just natural gas and electricity, but bandwidth, weather derivatives, and virtually any commodity that could be financialized. The company grew explosively. By 2000, Enron reported revenues of over $100 billion and was ranked seventh on the Fortune 500. Lei was celebrated as a visionary. He was a major political donor, contributing millions to both parties, but overwhelmingly to Republicans. He was close to the Bush family, serving on advisory committees and flying the first President Bush and his wife on Enron's corporate jet. He was proposed as a potential secretary of energy or secretary of the treasury under George W. Bush. Behind the soaring revenues and the political prestige, Enron's financial architecture was rotting. The company had created a labyrinth of specialurpose entities off balance sheet partnerships designed to hide debt and inflate earnings. Chief Financial Officer Andrew Fasto had constructed these entities with the knowledge and prosecutors later argued the encouragement of senior leadership including Lei. The partnerships allowed Enron to transfer losses off its books making the company appear far more profitable than it actually was. Billions of dollars in debt were concealed. Earnings were fabricated. and the stock price, which served as both the currency and the collateral for much of the scheme, kept rising. The collapse began in October 2001 when Enron disclosed a $618 million loss and a $1.2 billion reduction in shareholder equity. Within weeks, the company admitted to overstating earnings by nearly $600 million over the previous four years. The stock price, which had peaked above $90 per share, plummeted. By December, Enron had filed for bankruptcy. It was at the time the largest bankruptcy in American history. 20,000 employees lost their jobs. Many of them had invested their retirement savings in Enron stock through the company's 4001N plan. When the stock became worthless, they lost everything. The scale of the human devastation was staggering. People who had worked for the company for decades, people who had believed the asurances of their own CEO found themselves unemployed and financially ruined simultaneously. Lelay insisted that Enron's collapse was the result of a conspiracy by shortellers, rogue executives, and hostile media. He claimed he had not known about the accounting irregularities. He blamed his subordinates, particularly Fasto and CEO Jeffrey Skielling, who had resigned just months before the collapse. Prosecutors did not believe him. On July 7th, 2004, Lei was indicted by a federal grand jury in Houston on 11 counts of securities fraud, wire fraud, and making false and misleading statements. The trial of Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skielling began on January 30th, 2006. The trial lasted 4 months. Lei took the stand in his own defense and maintained his innocence throughout. He told the jury that Enron stock constituted 90% of his wealth and that his net worth was actually negative $250,000. He projected the image of a man who had been victimized by his own subordinates. The jury was not persuaded. On May 25th, 2006, Lei was found guilty on six counts of conspiracy and fraud. In a separate bench trial, the judge found him guilty on four additional counts. Sentencing was scheduled for October 2006. Lei never appeared. On July 5th, 2006, while vacationing at his home near Aspen, Colorado, Lei suffered a heart attack and died. He was 64 years old. The autopsy confirmed coronary artery disease. Conspiracy theories circulated immediately with some speculating that Lei had faked his death to avoid prison. There is no credible evidence supporting those theories because Lei died before his appeal could be resolved. The court vacated his conviction under the legal doctrine of abatement AB initio. In legal terms, it was as if the trial had never happened. The Department of Justice objected, but had no mechanism to override the doctrine. For the victims, it was a final insult. The man they held responsible for their ruin, would never serve a single day in prison, and his conviction, the one tangible result of years of investigation and prosecution, had been erased. The legislative aftermath of Enron was enormous. The Sarbain Oxley Act of 2002 imposed sweeping new requirements on corporate governance, financial disclosure, and executive accountability. CEOs and CFOs were now required to personally certify the accuracy of their financial statements. Independent audit committees were strengthened. Penalties for corporate fraud were dramatically increased. The law was a direct response to the Enron disaster and it remains one of the most significant pieces of financial regulation in modern American history. Lelay's memorial service was attended by more than a thousand guests, including former President George HW Bush and former Secretary of State James Baker. Speakers praised Lei as a devoted family man and a generous philanthropist. Outside the church, protesters gathered. The gap between those two realities, the eulogy and the protest, captured something essential about the story of Kenneth Lei. He was a man who had risen from rural poverty to the summit of American corporate power and who left behind a legacy that the most generous assessment can only describe as catastrophic. Number four, Bernie Ebers. He drove himself to prison in his own MercedesBenz. That detail reported in multiple news accounts from September 26th, 2006 says something about the particular stubbornness and self-image of Bernard Ebers, a man who refused to accept that the world he had built was a fraud even as the courts dismantled it piece by piece around him. He had been sentenced to 25 years in federal prison for presiding over an 11 billion accounting scandal at Worldcom, the largest such fraud in American history at the time. He appealed and lost. When the judge ordered him to report, he got behind the wheel and drove himself to the Oakdale Federal Correctional Institution in Louisiana, as if going to prison were just another appointment on his calendar. The collapse of WorldCom did not merely bankrupt a company. It destroyed the financial security of tens of thousands of employees and investors. It contributed to the broader erosion of public trust in American corporations that defined the early 2000s. And it led directly to the same wave of reform, including the Sarbain Oxley Act, that Enron's collapse had already set in motion. Bernard John Ebers was born on August 27th, 1941 in Edmonton, Alberta, the second of five children. His father, John, was a traveling salesman. His mother, Kathleen, was devoutly Christian. The family moved frequently during Ebers's childhood, first to California, then to a mission post on a Navajo Nation reservation in New Mexico, then back to Canada. It was an itinerant, religiously grounded upbringing that instilled in Ebers both a deep faith and a restless ambition to transcend his circumstances. He was not a strong student. He drifted between the University of Alberta and Calvin College before enrolling at Mississippi College on a basketball scholarship. A knee injury ended his playing career before his senior season, and he was reassigned to coach the junior varsity team. In 1967, he graduated with a bachelor's degree in physical education. It was not the credential of a future telecommunications mogul. But Ebers had something that no degree could confer. He had an instinct for deals, for growth, for the thrill of acquisition. He started in business by operating a chain of motel in Mississippi. The motel were modest, but they taught him about managing cash flow, about leverage, about the difference between owning something and making something work. In 1983, in a coffee shop in Hattisburg, Mississippi, Ebers and three other investors formed Long-distance Discount Services, a small telecommunications company. By 1985, Ebers had been named CEO. Over the next decade, he acquired more than 60 telecommunications companies, building LDDDS into a regional powerhouse. In 1995, the company changed its name to WorldCom. The acquisitions accelerated. In 1996, WorldCom purchased MFS Communications. In 1998, it acquired MCI Communications, one of the largest mergers in American history. Ebers became a titan of the telecom boom. He was worth an estimated $1.4 billion. He owned Canada's largest ranch, a 500,000 acre property in British Columbia. He owned timber companies, hotels, a yacht building firm, a trucking company, and a minor league hockey team. He taught Sunday school at East Haven Baptist Church in Brook Haven, Mississippi, and started corporate meetings with prayer. He was named to the Wired 25, the Time Digital 50, and the Mississippi Business Hall of Fame. Beneath the expansion, the financials were deteriorating. WorldCom's explosive growth through acquisitions had created a company that was far less profitable than it appeared. When the dotcom bubble burst in 2000 and when regulators blocked WorldCom's planned $115 billion acquisition of Sprint, the company's underlying weakness was exposed. Revenue growth slowed, earnings declined, and Ebers, whose personal wealth was heavily tied to WorldCom stock, was facing margin calls as the share price dropped. Rather than confront the reality of the situation, WorldCom's senior financial management, led by Chief Financial Officer Scott Sullivan, began manipulating the books. Line costs, the fees WorldCom paid to other companies to use their networks, were reclassified as capital expenditures, making them appear as long-term investments rather than operating expenses. This single accounting trick inflated WorldCom's earnings by billions of dollars. The fraud eventually totaled approximately 11 billion, making it the largest accounting scandal in American history. Ebers later claimed he had no knowledge of the accounting fraud that it was entirely the work of Sullivan and others beneath him. Sullivan, who cooperated with prosecutors in exchange for a reduced sentence, testified that Ebers had directed him to hit the numbers at any cost and had known about the manipulations. The question at the heart of the case was whether the CEO of the company had been ignorant of an 11 billion fraud taking place directly under his supervision. On June 25th, 2002, WorldCom announced that it had identified nearly $4 billion in accounting irregularities. The figure would eventually grow to 11 billion. On July 22nd, 2002, the company filed for bankruptcy. At the time, it was the largest bankruptcy filing in American corporate history, surpassing Enron. Ebers appeared before Congress on July 8th, 2002. He made a brief statement insisting he had nothing to hide, then invoked his fifth amendment right against self-inccrimination and refused to answer further questions. The committee threatened him with contempt charges, but did not follow through. On March 2nd, 2004, federal authorities indicted Ebers on securities fraud and conspiracy charges. The indictment was later expanded to include additional counts. On March 15, 2005, after a trial in which Sullivan served as the prosecution star witness, Ebers was found guilty on all counts. On July 13th, 2005, federal judge Barbara Jones sentenced him to 25 years in prison. The severity of the sentence shocked many observers, but the court held that it reflected the magnitude of the fraud and the devastation it had caused. investors brought a class action lawsuit that eventually resulted in a settlement of over $6 billion. Ebers was required to surrender virtually all of his assets, including his Mississippi home, his lumber company, his marina, his golf course, his hotel, and thousands of acres of timberland. After the settlement, his wife was left with an estimated $50,000. Ebers served 13 years before being granted compassionate release in December 2019 due to severe health problems. His lawyer said he was legally blind, suffering from dementia, anemia, and significant weight loss. He died at his home in Brook Haven, Mississippi on February 2nd, 2020 at the age of 78. The church where he had taught Sunday school did not issue a public statement. The community that had celebrated him as a self-made success. A devout Christian businessman who had put Brook Haven on the map absorbed his downfall quietly. WorldCom itself was reorganized and eventually merged with Verizon. The regulatory reforms it helped inspire endure. And the question that haunted the entire case, whether a CEO can build an empire on fraud while genuinely not knowing what his own financial officers are doing, has never been satisfactorily answered. Number five, Alan Stanford. His earliest possible release date is March 13, 213. That is not a typographical error. Robert Allen Stanford was sentenced to 110 years in federal prison for operating a 7 billion Ponzi scheme. A sentence so extreme that a federal prosecutor described it as the functional equivalent of economic homicide. At the time of his sentencing, Stanford denied everything. He blamed the government. He called the regulators who exposed him Gestapo. And then he was taken to a maximum security federal penitentiary in Florida where he will almost certainly spend every remaining day of his life. The effects of his fraud radiated across continents in Antigga and Barbuda, the tiny Caribbean nation where Stanford had based his offshore bank and cultivated himself as a combination of benefactor, employer, and kingmaker. The economy was devastated. Stanford International Bank had been one of the island's largest employers. His cricket tournaments had brought global attention and revenue. His newspapers had shaped public opinion. When the fraud was exposed, thousands of Antiguans lost their jobs and their savings simultaneously. The Caribbean Development Bank estimated that Antigua's GDP contracted by as much as 12% in the aftermath. In the United States, thousands of investors, many of them retirees who had been promised safe, above market returns on certificates of deposit, discovered that their money had been spent. Some never recovered. When the fraud was exposed in 2002, investigators found that the Rigus family had used Adelfia as a personal bank, borrowing billions of dollars through off-balance sheet entities, using company funds to purchase luxury condominiums to build a private golf course to finance timber rights and to fund family ventures that had nothing to do with the cable business. The collapse of Adelfia cost investors and creditors billions. and wiped out the company's 22,000 employees trust in their own leadership. The reverberations were felt across the cable industry and contributed to the broader crisis of confidence in American corporations during the early 2000s. Rig was born on November 14th, 1924 in Wellsville, New York to Greek immigrant parents. He booze tables by the age of nine. He served in the United States Army during World War II. He earned a bachelor's degree from Renolier Polytenic Institute. He purchased his first cable television franchise in countersport, Pennsylvania in 1952 when cable was a fledgling technology serving rural communities that could not receive broadcast signals. He grew the company methodically, acquiring franchises across smalltown America and building a reputation as a modest, hands-on operator who knew every corner of his business. The problems emerged when Rig began treating the company's finances as indistinguishable from his own family's finances. Offbalance sheet partnerships known as the Riga's family entities were used to borrow approximately $2.3 billion backed by Adelfia's credit but not disclosed to shareholders. The money was used for personal expenses, family business ventures and to cover margin calls on Adelfia stock held by family members. In 2002, Adelfia disclosed the offbalance sheet liabilities, triggering a collapse in the stock price and an SEC investigation. Company filed for bankruptcy in June 2002. In July 2004, a federal jury convicted John Riggus on charges of conspiracy, bank fraud, and securities fraud. His son Timothy was convicted on similar charges. John Riggus was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison. He was released in 2016 due to declining health and died in September 2021 at the age of 96. The Adelfia case became a study in the dangers of familycontrolled public companies that operate without adequate independent oversight. It reinforced the importance of board level governance reforms and the disclosure of related party transactions, principles that were strengthened by the corporate reform legislation of that era. Number 14, Rajat Gupta. The phone call lasted less than a minute. On September 23rd, 2008, Rajat Gupta, a member of the board of directors of Goldman Sachs, hung up after a board meeting in which the directors discussed a $5 billion investment from Warren Buffett's Burkshar Hathaway. Within minutes, his friend Raj Rajaratnam, the founder of the Gallian Group hedge fund, placed a massive order for Goldman Sachs stock. The timing was devastating in its clarity. Gupta had leaked inside information to Roger Ratnam and Rajar Ratnam had traded on it immediately. The call and the subsequent trade were captured through wiretaps that the FBI had placed on Roger Rottnham's phone as part of a broader investigation into insider trading on Wall Street. The evidence was not circumstantial. It was direct, recorded, and devastating. The fall of Rajat Gupta from the pinnacle of global business to a federal prison cell became one of the most dramatic and culturally significant white collar crime cases of the 21st century reshaping the way corporate boards financial regulators and law enforcement. Think about the responsibilities of fiduciary duty. Gupta was born in 1948 in Kolkata, India. He lost both parents by the time he was 18. He was admitted to the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, one of the most competitive universities in the world and later earned an MBA from Harvard Business School. He joined McKenzie and Company in 1973 and rose to become its managing director, the global leader of the most prestigious management consulting firm on Earth, a position he held for three consecutive terms from 1994 to 2003. He sat on the boards of Goldman Sachs, Proctor and Gamble and numerous other corporations and nonprofits. He was widely regarded as one of the most accomplished Indian-born business leaders in the world. His relationship with Raja Ratnam, a fellow South Asian business figure, proved to be his undoing. The SEC and the United States Attorney's Office alleged that Gupta had tipped Rajaratnam with material non-public information on multiple occasions, including details about Goldman Sachs's quarterly earnings and the Berkshire Hathaway investment. Roger Rottnham used the information to trade ahead of the announcements, generating millions of dollars in illegal profits. In October 2012, a federal jury convicted Gupta on four felony counts of conspiracy and securities fraud. He was sentenced to two years in federal prison and fined $5 million. He served 19 months and was released in 2016. The Gupta case established that corporate board members who leak confidential information can be prosecuted criminally, not merely sanctioned civily. It strengthened the legal framework around insider trading enforcement and demonstrated that no amount of professional prestige or philanthropic activity could immunize a person from the consequences of betraying a fiduciary trust. The case also prompted corporations and financial institutions to tighten their information security protocols and to educate board members about the legal boundaries of confidentiality. Number 15, Richard Scrushy. He beat the accounting fraud charges. That fact remains one of the most astonishing outcomes in the history of American white collar criminal prosecution. In June 2005, a jury in Birmingham, Alabama, acquitted Richard Scrushy of all 36 counts related to a $2.7 billion accounting fraud at Health South Corporation, the company he had founded. 14 of his former executives had already pleaded guilty and testified against him. The financial evidence was overwhelming, and yet the jury chose to believe Scrushy's defense that the fraud had been committed entirely by subordinates acting without his knowledge or direction. The acquitt did not save him. In 2006, Scrusi was convicted in a separate case of bribery and conspiracy related to a $500,000 payment to the governor of Alabama in exchange for a seat on a state regulatory board. He was sentenced to nearly 7 years in federal prison. In a civil ace, he was found liable for the Health South fraud and ordered to pay $2.87 billion. The combined outcome left scrushy, financially ruined, and legally disgraced. But the acquitt on the accounting charges remains a cautionary lesson about the difficulty of prosecuting CEOs who build layers of subordinates between themselves and the mechanics of fraud. Scrushy was born in August 1952 in Selma, Alabama. He trained as a respiratory therapist and worked his way into hospital administration. In 1984, he founded Health South Corporation, which grew into the nation's largest provider of outpatient surgery and rehabilitation services. Under Scrish's direction, beginning in the late 1990s, senior executives at HealthSouth inflated the company's earnings by over $2.5 billion through accounting manipulations designed to meet Wall Street expectations. The fraud was exposed in 2003 when the SEC filed charges. The case became a landmark in corporate governance debates about the responsibility of a CEO for the financial statements issued under their authority. The Health South scandal and its aftermath contributed to the growing consensus that executive accountability required not just criminal prosecution but structural reforms within corporate boards and audit committees. Number 16, Tom Peters. The purchase orders were fake. Every single one of them. Tom Peters operated a $3.65 billion Ponzi scheme through his company Peters Group Worldwide based in Minnotonka, Minnesota by creating fictitious purchase orders for consumer electronics. He told investors that their money was being used to buy merchandise, primarily computers and other electronics, at a discount, which would then be resold to major retailers at a profit. The goods did not exist. The retailers had no knowledge of the transactions. The documents were fabricated, and the returns paid to investors came entirely from money contributed by newer investors. The classic architecture of a Ponzi scheme. Peters was born in 1957 and grew up in Minnesota. He entered the electronics retail business in the 1980s and built a portfolio of companies including Polaroid Corporation, Sun Country Airlines, and Finger Hut. By the mid 2000s, he was one of the wealthiest businessmen in the state. with a lifestyle that reflected his purported success, multiple homes, private jets, and prominent philanthropic activity. The scheme was exposed in 2008 when a cooperating witness began recording conversations with Peters. The recordings captured Peters discussing the fabrication of documents and the mechanics of the fraud in explicit detail. He was indicted in December 2008 on multiple counts of mail fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy. In December 2009, a federal jury convicted him on all 20 counts. In April 2010, he was sentenced to 50 years in federal prison, effectively a life sentence. The Pett's case was the largest Ponzi scheme to originate in the Midwest and the second largest in American history at the time. The courtapp appointed receiver spent more than a decade recovering assets for victims, ultimately distributing over $722 million. The case underscored the vulnerability of investors to sophisticated fabrication schemes and the importance of independent verification of the assets underlying investment returns. Number 17, Trevor Milton. The truck rolled down a hill. That was the revelation that crystallized everything. In September 2020, Hindenburg Research, a shortselling firm, published a report alleging that Nicola Corporation, the electric and hydrogen truck startup founded by Trevor Milton, was an intricate fraud built on dozens of lies. Among the most memorable allegations was that a promotional video showing a Nickeola prototype truck in motion had been staged by towing the vehicle to the top of a hill and filming it as it rolled down under the force of gravity. The truck had no functioning drivetrain. It could not move under its own power. The video had been used to attract investors and to support Milton's claims that the company had achieved technological breakthroughs that in reality did not exist. Milton was born on April 6th, 1982 and grew up in Utah. He did not complete a college degree. His early career included a home alarm company and a natural gas company called the Hybrid, neither of which achieved significant success. In 2014, he founded Nicola Motor Company, named after the inventor Nicola Tesla with the stated goal of producing zero emission trucks powered by hydrogen fuel cells and batteries. Milton was a charismatic pitchman who made bold claims about the company's technology on social media, in press conferences, and in investor presentations. He said Nicola had developed proprietary hydrogen technology that would revolutionize the trucking industry. He claimed the company was years ahead of its competitors. He attracted billions of dollars in investment. In June 2020, Nicola went public through a reverse merger with a specialurpose acquisition company, briefly achieving a market capitalization greater than that of Ford Motor Company. After the Hindenburg report was published, Milton resigned as executive chairman. Federal prosecutors and the SEC launched investigations. In July 2021, Milton was indicted on securities fraud and wire fraud charges. The trial took place in 2022. Prosecutors presented evidence that Milton had made false statements about nearly every aspect of the company's technology, partnerships, and production capabilities. On October 14th, 2022, the jury convicted him on three of four fraud charges. He was sentenced to four years in federal prison. In March 2025, Milton received a presidential pardon. The pardon drew criticism from investor advocates and legal experts who argued it undermined accountability for securities fraud. Nicola itself eventually filed for bankruptcy. The case became a cautionary tale about the risks of investing in companies based primarily on the charisma and claims of their founders rather than on verified technology and audited financial results. Number 18, Martin Wintercorn. 11 million vehicles. That was the number. 11 million diesel cars worldwide had been equipped with software specifically designed to cheat emissions tests. The device detected when the vehicle was being tested and activated emissions controls that reduced nitrogen oxide output to comply with regulatory standards. During normal driving, the controls were deactivated and the vehicles emitted pollutants at levels up to 40 times higher than the legal limit. The scale of the deception was almost incomprehensible. Volkswagen, one of the world's largest and most respected automakers, a company synonymous with German engineering, had systematically deceived regulators, customers, and the public for years. The fallout reshaped the global automotive industry, accelerated the transition to electric vehicles, destroyed tens of billions of dollars in shareholder value, and led to criminal charges, convictions, and regulatory penalties across multiple continents. Martin Winterorn was born on June 24th, 1947 in Leonberg, Germany. He studied methology and metal physics, earning a doctorate and built his career within the Volkswagen Group, rising through the ranks to become CEO in 2007. Under his leadership, Volkswagen pursued an aggressive strategy to overtake Toyota as the world's largest automaker by volume. Central to that strategy was the expansion of diesel vehicle sales in the United States, where diesel had traditionally been less popular than in Europe. The problem was that Volkswagen's diesel engines could not meet American emissions standards without sacrificing the performance and fuel efficiency that were central to the brand's appeal. Rather than solve the engineering challenge, employees developed defeat device software that would detect the specific conditions of an emissions test and adjust the engine's behavior accordingly. The deception was eventually uncovered by researchers at West Virginia University who conducted realworld emissions testing and found massive discrepancies between laboratory results and on-road performance. In September 2015, the Environmental Protection Agency issued a notice of violation to Volkswagen. Winterorn resigned within days. He publicly denied any personal knowledge of the cheating scheme. Prosecutors in the United States indicted him in May 2018 on charges of conspiracy and wire fraud. Because he resides in Germany, which does not extradite its own citizens, he has not faced trial in the United States. In Germany, criminal proceedings against Winterorn began in September 2024. He faces charges of fraud, market manipulation, and false testimony before a parliamentary committee. Volkswagen has paid more than $30 billion in fines, settlements, and vehicle buybacks worldwide. Several lower ranking employees and executives have been convicted in related proceedings. The scandal prompted the European Union to overhaul its vehicle emissions testing regime and accelerated policy discussions about the phase out of internal combustion engines. It also exposed the limitations of regulatory testing protocols that had been designed to detect fraud but had failed to do so for years. The consequences continue to accumulate not just for Volkswagen but for an entire industry that was forced to confront the gap between its public image and its private practices. Number 19, Jeffrey Skielling. He told his Harvard Business School classmates that the most important thing in business was to do deals and make money. The quote recounted in multiple accounts of his early career foreshadowed everything that followed. Jeffrey Skielling was the intellectual architect of Enron's transformation from a pipeline company into a trading empire. The man who built the mark-to-market accounting framework that allowed Enron to book future profits immediately. The man whose relentless drive for financial innovation created the conditions in which fraud could not only thrive but become the operating principle of the entire organization. Skiilling was born on November 25th, 1953 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He was raised in a middleclass family in Aurora, Illinois. He attended Southern Methodist University and then Harvard Business School where he graduated as a Baker Scholar, a distinction reserved for the top 5% of the class. He joined McKenzie and Company, the elite consulting firm, where he eventually became a partner and led the firm's energy practice. It was through McKenzie that he met Kenneth Lei and began advising Enron. Skiilling joined Enron in 1990 as head of Enron Finance Corp. and quickly became the most influential executive at the company. He championed the concept of an asset light energy company, one that traded energy contracts rather than building and maintaining physical infrastructure. He introduced mark-to-market accounting, which allowed Enron to record projected profits from long-term contracts at the time the deals were signed rather than as the revenue was actually earned. The practice was approved by Enron's auditor, Arthur Anderson, and by the SEC, but its application at Enron was stretched far beyond any reasonable interpretation of accounting standards. Under skilling, Enron created increasingly complex financial instruments and specialurpose entities designed to move debt off the balance sheet and inflate earnings. The culture inside the company became ruthlessly competitive. Employees were evaluated under a rank and yank system in which the lowest performing workers were fired annually. The result was an environment in which reporting bad news was career suicide and in which the appearance of profitability became more important than its reality. Skiilling was named CEO of Enron in February 2001. He resigned abruptly in August 2001, citing personal reasons just months before the company's collapse. His resignation came at a time when the cracks in Enron's finances were already becoming visible to insiders. Prosecutors later argued that Skielling resigned because he knew the fraud was about to be exposed. In February 2004, Skielling was indicted on 35 counts of fraud, conspiracy, and insider trading. His trial conducted jointly with Kenneth Lei lasted from January to May 2006. On May 25th, 2006, the jury convicted skilling on 19 of 28 counts, including conspiracy, securities fraud, and insider trading. He was sentenced to 24 years in prison and fined $45 million. In 2013, the Department of Justice agreed to reduce Skilling's sentence to 14 years as part of a deal that also required him to forfeit $42 million to be distributed to victims of the fraud. He was released from federal prison in 2019 after serving approximately 12 years. His conviction was never overturned. The legacy of skilling at Enron is inseparable from the legacy of Enron itself. He was the operational mind behind the company's most aggressive and ultimately fraudulent practices. His prosecution and conviction established that the intellectual architects of corporate fraud, not just the financial officers who carry out the mechanics, can be held criminally responsible. The Enron case, driven in large part by Skiillings innovations, reshaped American corporate law, accounting standards, and the regulatory framework governing public companies. Number 20, Richard Sackler. No member of the Sackler family has been criminally charged. That fact, more than any other defines the legacy of Purdue Pharma and its role in the American opioid epidemic. the company that manufactured Oxycontton, the prescription painkiller that became the gateway drug for a crisis that has killed more than 500,000 Americans. Pleaded guilty to federal criminal charges, not once, but twice. Billions of dollars in settlements have been paid. Thousands of lawsuits have been filed. Congressional hearings have produced devastating testimony. And yet the family that owned the company, that directed its marketing strategy, that pushed its sales force to maximize prescriptions, that reaped more than $10 billion in profits as the death toll mounted, has never faced a criminal trial. The consequences of Purdue Pharma and the Sackler's conduct are measured not in dollars, but in lives. The opioid epidemic has reshaped American public health, criminal justice, and social policy on a scale comparable to the great epidemics of the 19th century. Entire communities, particularly in Appalachia, the Midwest, and rural New England have been devastated. Hospitals, emergency rooms, foster care systems, and morgs have been overwhelmed. The crisis prompted the creation of new treatment programs, new law enforcement strategies, new nlloxxone distribution programs, and new litigation frameworks. And at the center of it all, the family whose product lit the fuse has remained legally untouched by criminal accountability. Richard Sackler was born in 1945 in Roslin, New York. He was the son of Raymond Sackler, one of three brothers who purchased the pharmaceutical company that would become Purdue Pharma in the 1950s. All three brothers were physicians. Richard joined the company in 1971 and eventually rose to become its president. He was not a passive inheritor. Internal documents revealed during litigation showed that Richard Sackler was deeply involved in the strategy to market Oxycontton as aggressively as possible. Oxycontton was approved by the FDA in 1995 and launched in 1996. Purdue Pharma marketed the drug with a campaign that was in retrospect a masterpiece of pharmaceutical deception. The company told doctors that Oxycontton's timerelease formulation made it less addictive than other opioids. Sales representatives downplayed the risk of addiction. Marketing materials emphasized the drug's effectiveness for chronic pain and minimized its dangers. Internal communications disclosed during lawsuits showed that Purdue's leadership, including Richard Sackler, was aware of the drug's addictive potential and of the growing evidence of abuse, and that the company chose to continue marketing aggressively rather than pull back. As Oxycontton prescriptions soared, so did addiction, overdose, and death. Patients who became addicted to the prescription drug often transitioned to cheaper and more accessible opioids, including heroin and illicitly manufactured fentinel. The epidemic cascaded across the country. In 2007, Purdue Pharma and three of its executives pleaded guilty to federal charges of misbranding Oxycontton. The company paid $600 million in fines and penalties. The three executives received probation and fines, but no prison time. The guilty plea addressed only the company's marketing conduct prior to 2006. In 2020, Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty again, this time to three federal criminal charges, including conspiracy to defraud the United States and violating federal anti- kickback laws. The company agreed to pay $8.3 billion, though much of that amount was uncollectible because Purdue had already filed for bankruptcy. No individual Sackler family member was named in the criminal charges. The Sackler family agreed to pay up to $6.5 billion over 15 years as part of a broader settlement with state and local governments. In exchange, the family received protection from future civil lawsuits. The Supreme Court initially blocked the deal in 2024, ruling that the bankruptcy process could not be used to grant immunity to non-deptorters, but a revised settlement was reached in 2025. Richard Sackler and other family members have never admitted personal wrongdoing. The absence of individual criminal charges against the Sacklers has become one of the most controversial aspects of the entire opioid crisis. Critics argue that the legal system failed to hold the people most responsible for the epidemic accountable. Defenders of the outcome argue that the evidence, while damning, did not meet the standard required for criminal prosecution of individuals under existing law. The debate has fueled calls for reforms in corporate criminal liability and for new legal tools to pierce the protections that wealthy individuals can deploy to shield themselves from prosecution. The name Sackler once affixed to museums, galleries, and university buildings around the world has been systematically removed by institutions seeking to distance themselves from the family's legacy. The Louvre, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Guggenheim, and numerous universities have taken down the name. But the epidemic continues. The death toll continues to rise. And the question of whether the architects of a catastrophe that has killed hundreds of thousands of people will ever face criminal justice remains as of this writing unanswered.
fullTextVi: Số một, Elizabeth Holmes. Sự lừa đảo mà cô xây dựng đã không sụp đổ một cách rầm rộ. Nó hòa tan từ từ, từng phân tử, giống như mẫu máu mà máy của cô ấy cho là để phân tích, nhưng không bao giờ có thể. Khi lớp bụi cuối cùng đã lắng xuống Therronos, những gì còn lại không chỉ đơn thuần là thất bại công ty. Đó là một vết sẹo vĩnh viễn trên khuôn mặt Thung lũng Silicon, một vết thương trong cuộc trò chuyện quốc gia về sự đổi mới, tham vọng và ranh giới giữa tầm nhìn và sự lừa dối. Các nhà lập pháp sẽ viết lại các tiêu chuẩn giám sát. Nhà đầu tư ủy thác hàng trăm triệu USD cho một phụ nữ từng tung hô như Steve Jobs tiếp theo sẽ dành nhiều năm kiện tụng để cố gắng thu lại từng xu về những gì họ đã đánh mất. Và những bệnh nhân nhận được kết quả xét nghiệm máu không chính xác, một số người trong số họ bị bệnh nặng, còn lại tự hỏi liệu các phương pháp điều trị mà bác sĩ của họ đã kê đơn có dựa trên dữ liệu bị lỗi hay không đã làm hại họ nhiều hơn là có lợi. Hậu quả của Elizabeth Holmes tỏa ra bên ngoài như những vết nứt trên kính, và chúng có lan tỏa chưa xong. Cô sinh ngày 3 tháng 2 năm 1984 tại Washington, D. C. trong một gia đình hiểu rõ cơ chế quyền lực của Mỹ. Cha cô, Christian Holmes, nắm giữ các vị trí điều hành trong chính phủ liên bang, bao gồm cả các vai trò tại USAD, Cơ quan Bảo vệ Môi trường và Cơ quan Thương mại và Phát triển Hoa Kỳ. Trước đó, ông từng là phó chủ tịch của Enron, một công ty có vụ lừa đảo ngoạn mục một ngày nào đó sẽ trở thành một bài hát đen tối đối với câu chuyện của con gái ông. Mẹ cô, Noel Dowst, từng là nhân viên ủy ban quốc hội. Hai bên gia đình đều có sự giàu có và dòng dõi. Gia đình Holmes có nguồn gốc từ Charles Louie Fleshman, một người nhập cư Hungary đã thành lập Fleshman's Chist và xây dựng nên một trong những vận may công nghiệp vĩ đại của Mỹ vào thế kỷ 19 thế kỷ. Một người bạn của gia đình từng nói rằng gia đình Holmes rất tự hào về lịch sử đó, tự hào của đế chế men, và Elizabeth đã nuôi tham vọng đòi lại điều đó trạng thái từ khi còn rất trẻ. Cô theo học trường St. John ở Houston, một trong những trường tư thục uy tín nhất thành phố, nơi cô nổi bật nhờ sự quyết tâm hơn là sự ấm áp. Cô không được nhớ đến là người đặc biệt hòa đồng. Cô được nhớ đến như một người không ngừng nghỉ. Khi còn học trung học, cô đã tự học tiếng Quan Thoại và bắt đầu theo học tại Stanford Chương trình ngôn ngữ mùa hè của trường đại học. Cô tuyên bố đã bắt đầu kinh doanh bán trình biên dịch C++ cho các trường đại học Trung Quốc trước đây cô ấy thậm chí đã tốt nghiệp. Cho dù tuyên bố đó có hoàn toàn chính xác hay không thì nó cũng đã thiết lập một khuôn mẫu theo cô ấy trong hai thập kỷ tiếp theo. Elizabeth Holmes đã hiểu được sức mạnh của việc kể chuyện ngay từ khi còn rất trẻ. Cô ấy hiểu rằng câu chuyện bạn kể về bản thân có thể quan trọng hơn sản phẩm bạn thực sự xây dựng. Năm 2002, cô đăng ký vào Đại học Stanford để học ngành kỹ thuật hóa học. Sau năm thứ nhất, cô làm việc trong phòng thí nghiệm tại Viện Gen của Singapore, nơi cô xét nghiệm mẫu máu để tìm virus SARS Corona. Sau này cô ấy nói rằng chính ở đó, hạt giống của Theronos đã được gieo trồng. Cô gặp rắc rối với quá trình rườm rà khi lấy một lượng lớn máu bằng ống tiêm. Cô tưởng tượng ra một tương lai trong đó tất cả những thứ đó có thể được thay thế bằng chích một ngón tay. Một giọt máu nhỏ được phân tích trên thiết bị di động có khả năng chạy hàng trăm của các bài kiểm tra cùng một lúc. Tầm nhìn thật say sưa. Như nhiều chuyên gia đã nói với cô vào thời điểm đó, điều đó cũng không hợp lý về mặt khoa học. Khi Holmes trình bày ý tưởng này với Phyllis Gardner, giáo sư y khoa tại Stanford, Gardner trực tiếp nói với cô ấy rằng ý tưởng này sẽ không hiệu quả. Đơn giản là hóa sinh của máu không ủng hộ quan điểm cho rằng kết quả chẩn đoán có ý nghĩa có thể được bắt nguồn từ những mẫu nhỏ như vậy. Một số chuyên gia y tế khác tại trường đại học cũng nói điều tương tự. Holmes phớt lờ tất cả. Cô đã tìm được một người ủng hộ, Channing Robertson, trưởng khoa Kỹ thuật của Stanford, người đã đồng ý ủng hộ tầm nhìn của cô ấy. Vào tháng 3 năm 2004, ở tuổi 19, Holmes bỏ học ở Stanford, sử dụng tiền học phí của cô ấy làm nguồn tài trợ ban đầu và thành lập công ty mà sau này sẽ là tên là Theronos. Tên này là sự kết hợp của từ trị liệu và chẩn đoán. Tên ban đầu của phương pháp chữa bệnh theo thời gian thực đã bị loại bỏ vì có quá nhiều người nghi ngờ của từ chữa bệnh. Ngay cả ở giai đoạn đặt tên, Holmes đã quản lý được nhận thức. Đến tháng 12 năm 2004, Holmes đã huy động được 6 triệu USD. Đến năm 2010, Therronos đã thu hút được hơn 92 triệu USD vốn đầu tư mạo hiểm. Công nghệ vẫn chưa hoạt động nhưng tiền vẫn tiếp tục đến vì câu chuyện không thể cưỡng lại được. Leo Dennis Koslowski sinh ngày 16 tháng 11 năm 1946 tại Newark, New Jersey. Cha anh là một sĩ quan cảnh sát. Gia đình thuộc tầng lớp lao động. Koslowski không lớn lên với đặc quyền. Thực tế đằng sau hình ảnh còn xấu hơn nhiều. Klowski và giám đốc tài chính của ông, Mark Schwarz, đã xây dựng một hệ thống làm giàu bản thân hoạt động phần lớn ngoài tầm nhìn của ban giám đốc. Họ ủy quyền cho mình những khoản tiền thưởng mà chưa bao giờ được ủy ban bồi thường chấp thuận. Họ bán cổ phiếu công ty thông qua các kế hoạch nhằm lách các yêu cầu về tiết lộ thông tin. Và họ tiêu tiền của công ty vào những thú vui cá nhân một cách không chút kiềm chế. Ông là người đồng sáng lập quỹ phòng hộ Elilia Capital Management, quỹ này không tồn tại được lâu. Năm 2009, anh thành lập MSNB Capital Management cùng với một người bạn thuở nhỏ.
